name: walker
author: LLM, from a scenario. It asks for MOVEMENT. It does not ask for legs, and it does not ask for a gait.
scenario: A body that MOVES itself across the ground under real gravity, contact and friction. Go somewhere and keep going. This is the objective that cannot be faked: static stability could always be gamed with outriggers, but OUTRIGGERS DO NOT WALK. A lollipop cannot chase anything. Nothing here says how to move — walk, hop, slither, roll, gallop. If the universe has a better idea than mine, I want to be told.

constraints.why: THE GATE. NaN, a body flung to infinity, a degenerate rig. A physics glitch is not a gait, and if we do not gate it the optimiser WILL find it — that is the one thing it is reliably good at.

THE SECOND GATE, and it is pre-emptive: the classic exploit here is BALLISTIC LAUNCH — coil up, fire yourself down the field, and bank the distance. That is not locomotion, it is artillery. The body must stay in contact with the ground for most of the run.

THE THIRD GATE, and it is a REPAIR (2026-07-14). The first run produced a BRISTLEBOT: 8 microscopic bones (two of length exactly 0.00), buzzing at the maximum 5 Hz and ratcheting along on friction asymmetry. It worked because of TWO bugs of mine. (1) The mass floor was 50 g, so a bone of r=1mm, L=1cm — true mass 25 MICROGRAMS — was handed the density of neutron-star matter; every bone was pinned at that floor, so they all weighed the same regardless of size, and the physics was a lie. (2) `distance` is measured in BODY LENGTHS, so SHRINKING YOURSELF inflates the score for free. It did not learn to walk. It learned to be small and dense. This gate now rejects any body with zero-length stubs, hair-thin limbs, or a total size outside 0.8–6.0 m — so body-length normalisation, which IS the right metric in locomotion research, is only ever applied between COMPARABLE bodies.

THE POINT. Net displacement in BODY LENGTHS, so it cannot win by simply being enormous. `maximize`, not a band — a spec made only of walls gets you exactly the walls, and I have already been burned by a satisficer once today. Falling over is worth about one body length, and only once, so this term excludes toppling all by itself.
net displacement over path length. A creature that spins in place travels a long way and arrives nowhere.

metabolic cost. Thrashing every joint at full torque is a real way to move and a bad way to be alive. ... RECALIBRATED 2026-07-16 (ref 400.0 -> 12.0): measured 12.12; ref 400 gave sat 0.971 — 33x too high in the OTHER direction, so the term was DEAD and the winner never had to be cheap. Two refs in one repo, wrong by 89x and 33x in opposite directions, is proof neither was calibrated against a measurement. Set AT the measurement so metabolic cost actually pulls.
an animal, not a stick and not a hairball.

THE ANTI-LOTTERY (added 2026-07-16, the same day walker.measure() finally got restarts). worst/mean across N randomized starts: a real gait converges onto the same behaviour from every start (~1.0); a lucky roll does not (~0). MEASURED ON THE INCUMBENT: 0.6298 — the FIXED BODY that brain_cpu loads as 'grown once, reused for every brain, forever' loses 52% of its recorded 6.81 body lengths to a 2 cm nudge, and would FAIL brain_gpu's identical 0.75 floor. Every brain this studio has trained stands on a body selected by a coin toss. HARD, because a body that only works from one exact pose is not a body — it is that pose, and no brain standing on it can be measured honestly either. Note this cannot be satisfied by tuning any number: robustness is a ratio ACROSS rollouts, so the optimiser can only satisfy it STRUCTURALLY, by finding a body that actually stands up.
